{"id": "53:34/q03", "question": "What does akdā mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether the verb denotes cessation after giving, difficult refusal, reproach that spoils a gift, dwindling yield, or the gift's smallness; Bint al-Shāṭiʾ uses the coordination and poem's explicit bi-mannihi to separate these.", "positions": [{"id": "53:34/q03/p1", "position": "He stopped, cut off, or withheld what he had begun giving or doing.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUbayda, Ibn Qutayba, Mujāhid, al-Zajjāj, al-Thaʿlabī, al-Kisāʾī, al-Farrāʾ, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Abū Isḥāq, and later commentators trace it to a digger encountering an impenetrable hard layer in a well and giving up; Ibn Qutayba, Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn extend it to any unfinished endeavor. Al-Ḥuṭayʾa's verse illustrates a small gift followed by cessation while praising generosity. Other Arabic examples involve rock or mountain, exhausted fingers or hand, thick nails, and meager plant or house yield. Al-Rāzī prefers the related idiom 'I repelled him'; Bursevī cites Qāmūs and Tāj al-maṣādir. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ prefers stinginess after the small gift because the coordinated verbs require a new sense."}, {"id": "53:34/q03/p2", "position": "He made the gift difficult, refused firmly, or imposed hard terms.", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd cites bargaining and Arabic usages of hard digging, rough nails, weary fingers, and scant plant yield. Al-Naḥḥās speaks of obstructing the recipient; al-Mubarrad says forceful refusal. Kuran Yolu understands rigidity as extreme stinginess and an imposing attitude."}, {"id": "53:34/q03/p3", "position": "He spoiled the little gift by reproaching its recipient.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās adduces Arabic poetry, an unnamed poet says giving little followed by reproach contrasts with praiseworthy kindness, and al-Suyūṭī uses that poem. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ says the poem's reproach is explicit in bi-mannihi and cannot be read into thumma akdā itself."}, {"id": "53:34/q03/p4", "position": "It describes a small or dwindling yield or good.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī notes a plant with little yield and, via Abū Zayd, land with delayed growth; Abū Ḥayyān cites diminished house income and Abū Zayd's description of a man's dwindled generosity."}, {"id": "53:34/q03/p5", "position": "Akdā itself means a small gift.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ attributes this to al-Rāghib but argues the coordination with 'gave a little' requires a distinct meaning."}]}
{"id": "53:34/q04", "question": "How is the final alif read in this word?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "53:34/q04/p1", "position": "Abū ʿAmr reads listed nonfinal words with an open vowel on routes that incline verse endings.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazarī adds that for Mūsā Abū ʿAmr follows his usual between-vowels pronunciation where imāla is transmitted; the note does not explicitly name akdā."}]}
{"id": "53:34/q05", "question": "Who is depicted, according to the reports and explanations?", "turns_on": "Whether the relative expression points to a recoverable historical incident or sketches a type; reports name several people and differ on the exchange, while Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Rāzī, Ālūsī, Islahi and Kuran Yolu challenge particular reports.", "positions": [{"id": "53:34/q05/p1", "position": "Al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra, who responded to the Prophet but was dissuaded and paid a man claiming to bear his punishment.", "reasons": "Mujāhid and Ibn Zayd are frequent transmitters; al-Bayḍāwī calls this the majority account, while al-Ālūsī prefers it as best known and most fitting with 53:35. Reports vary between his following, accepting, or nearing Islam; the reproacher invokes ancestral religion, offers to bear punishment for money, and receives only part. Al-Ṭabarī's Ibn Zayd adds bargaining and a witnessed written agreement. Muqātil instead speaks of brief verbal good. Islahi says the account lacks a sound chain and fits the verses poorly; Kuran Yolu disputes the reliability and Quranic fit of such episodes."}, {"id": "53:34/q05/p2", "position": "ʿUthmān, whose foster brother ʿAbd Allāh ibn Saʿd ibn Abī Sarḥ induced him to curtail charity in return for assuming his sins.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Suddī, al-Kalbī and al-Musayyib transmit the account: ʿUthmān gave a camel, sometimes with gear, stopped or reduced charity, then resumed it; al-Thaʿlabī links turning away to Uḥud. Al-Zamakhsharī adds a witnessed deal; one report calls the brother maternal. Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls it false and says ʿUthmān is innocent; al-Rāzī finds it unestablished and contrary to his character; al-Ālūsī calls it baseless; Ibn ʿĀshūr relays Ibn ʿAṭiyya's objection that ʿUthmān would not heed him."}, {"id": "53:34/q05/p3", "position": "Al-ʿĀṣ ibn Wāʾil, who sometimes agreed with the Prophet; the gift may be money.", "reasons": "Al-Suddī is repeatedly cited for his partial agreement; Ibn ʿAbbās is separately reported to identify al-ʿĀṣ. Ibn ʿAṭiyya specifies money in al-Suddī's view."}, {"id": "53:34/q05/p4", "position": "Abū Jahl, who acknowledged the nobility of Muhammad's commands but did not believe.", "reasons": "Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Quraẓī is the transmitter; the reported verbal assent concerns noble manners or character."}, {"id": "53:34/q05/p5", "position": "Al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith, who paid five camels to a poor emigrant after apostasy and promised to bear his sin.", "reasons": "Al-Ḍaḥḥāk supplies the identification and five-camel detail; al-Ālūsī and Ibn ʿĀshūr repeat it."}, {"id": "53:34/q05/p6", "position": "An unnamed convert whose former associate offered to take his punishment for payment.", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd reports pressure to return to ancestral religion, additional payment demanded, and a witnessed written agreement; the later narrations preserve these details without naming him."}, {"id": "53:34/q05/p7", "position": "An unnamed man seeking a mount for an expedition, offered transport in exchange for another's sins or good deeds.", "reasons": "ʿIkrima says a friend lent a camel in exchange for taking on the friend's sins. Darrāj instead says the Prophet could not provide transport and another man supplied a mount to catch the army, with the passage extending through 53:41; the accounts differ in who assumes whose sins."}, {"id": "53:34/q05/p8", "position": "An unnamed man heading to the Prophet for good who surrendered his provisions to a pagan offering to bear his sin.", "reasons": "ʿAṭāʾ ibn Yasār reports the exchange; unlike the expedition reports, the man is on his way to visit the Prophet."}, {"id": "53:34/q05/p9", "position": "A person who disbelieved after believing.", "reasons": "Al-Nasafī attributes this application to Ibn ʿAbbās without naming the person."}, {"id": "53:34/q05/p10", "position": "A representative, hypothetical miserly idolater, standing for wealthy Quraysh and similarly presumptuous people.", "reasons": "Islahi argues that al-ladhī and al may introduce a parable rather than a historical individual; 16:92's woman unraveling yarn is his analogy. Walīd, Abū Jahl and others would recognize themselves in it. He disputes the unsound, ill-fitting al-Walīd story and the assumption that a relative pronoun requires a proper-name referent. Study Quran allows application to anyone neglecting others' needs."}]}
{"id": "53:34/q06", "question": "What fault or lesson does this act illustrate?", "turns_on": "Whether the criticism chiefly concerns imagined transfer of sins and apostasy, meager interrupted generosity and false confidence in reward, or a broken payment promise; Bursevī and Islahi explicitly challenge competing emphases.", "positions": [{"id": "53:34/q06/p1", "position": "Turning from faith while trusting a paid promise to transfer one's afterlife punishment is the central error.", "reasons": "Bursevī prefers this focus and calls cessation of the gift incidental and ironic; 53:35 challenges supposed knowledge of the unseen. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the man implicitly recognized turning away as a crime but wrongly assumed its consequences could be transferred. Al-Rāzī says money cannot carry another's sins. Biqāʿī infers that no one can know God's future judgment even of oneself, much less certify another's standing. Asad asks how limited giving proves there is no judgment."}, {"id": "53:34/q06/p2", "position": "Stinginess, breaking off generosity, and presuming a favorable standing in the Hereafter are censured.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr sees even small-scale stinginess as blame beyond disbelief; Islahi portrays those who assume Abrahamic or Mosaic descent ensures Paradise while ignoring those prophets' teaching and sacrifice. His misers give under pressure, then clench their fists and attack exhorters; 90:6 records their boast of vast spending. Kuran Yolu sees fleeting compassion overtaken by worldly attachment. Study Quran says interrupted good may nullify earlier efforts, like a well never reaching water. Bursevī rejects Muqātil's small donation to companions as disconnected from following verses."}, {"id": "53:34/q06/p3", "position": "The giver's stopping after a promise is blameworthy even if payment was not owed.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī answers the objection that a voluntary gift could harmlessly stop: noble Arab custom honors promises, and the proposed payment could never transfer sins. Islahi objects that the Qurʾān is not censuring al-Walīd for a broken promise."}, {"id": "53:34/q06/p4", "position": "A seeker who abandons a little spiritual striving for pleasure reveals unreadiness for union.", "reasons": "Bursevī treats life's capital as the resource briefly spent on the path before the sensual ego reclaims it."}]}

{"id": "53:35/q04", "question": "What unseen matter does the question challenge him to know?", "turns_on": "Which hidden claim his conduct presumes: transferable punishment, future poverty, his reward, the truth of revelation, resurrection, or hidden knowledge more generally. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī prefers the worldly-future reading because 53:38 itself addresses transfer of sins.", "positions": [{"id": "53:35/q04/p1", "position": "Whether another person can bear his sins or punishment for him.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās, al-Wāḥidī, al-Baghawī, al-Ṭabrisī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Nasafī, Abū Ḥayyān, Bursevī, al-Ālūsī, Elmalılı, and Ibn ʿĀshūr apply the question to his companion's undertaking.
